title: The widow of Naim (Luke 7:11–17)
hookLine: Jesus stops a funeral because he had compassion on the mother

lines: TWO CROWDS AT A TOWN GATE.
AN ONLY SON, A WIDOWED MOTHER.
cards: Two crowds meet at a town gate. One is coming out: a funeral, with a large crowd from the town walking beside the bier. On it lies a young man, the only son of his mother, and she is a widow.
The other crowd is coming in, following Jesus and his disciples up the road. The town is Naim. Nobody asks Jesus for anything.

teach.b: Luke tells it in seven verses.
The turning point: "And when the Lord had seen her, being moved with mercy towards her, he said to her: Weep not." Look at the order. He sees her first.
Not the dead son, the mother. Luke has already told us what is at stake for her: she is a widow, and this was her only son. Then he's moved.

Luke's Greek word for it comes from the word for the inner organs, the gut: the feeling that grabs you in the stomach. Then he speaks to her: weep not. Only then does he touch the bier, and the bearers stop.
"Young man, I say to thee, arise."

teach.h: HE GAVE HIM TO HIS MOTHER.
teach.b: The young man sits up and begins to speak, and Luke adds the gentlest line in the story: he delivered him to his mother. Not to the crowd. To her.
The people respond with fear and praise: a great prophet has risen among us, and God has visited his people.
Readers hear an echo of Elias, who raised a widow's son at Sarephta long before, in the Third Book of Kings in the Douay.
Luke is the only Gospel that tells this story, and he notices widows again and again: Anna in the Temple, the widow who keeps coming back to an unjust judge, the widow with two small coins.
Catholics hear it as a picture of how God looks at grief. Before anything is fixed, someone sees you, is moved, and speaks to you.
Weep not isn't a scolding. It's what you say to a person when you're about to help.

how: Comforting the sorrowful is one of the Church's spiritual works of mercy, and some Catholic parishes send people to sit with grieving families, bring meals, and pray with them at the funeral vigil.

games.q: you're walking into a town and meet a funeral coming out. a widow is following her only son's body. nobody has asked you for anything. what do you do?
o: step aside respectfully and let them pass.
speak to the mother first: weep not.
games.why: he speaks to her before he does anything else, then touches the bier and raises her son, and gives him back to her.

practice: Think of someone you know who is grieving right now: a death, a divorce, a diagnosis, a child far away.

Picture them the way Jesus saw the widow at the gate, let yourself feel it in the gut, and think of one small thing that might help: a message, a meal, sitting with them, saying the name of the one they lost.
If you pray, hold them before God.

wordCard.voice: Naim. The town gate where a widow's only son lay on the bier, and Jesus saw her, moved with compassion, before anyone asked. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: he was moved with compassion, from splanchna, the inner organs: mercy felt in the gut.

carryVoice: Your line: weep not. That's week sixty-five, from two coats to the gate of Naim. Day four hundred fifty-five, done.
